# DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development (2025)

**Source:** DORA (Google Cloud), *State of AI-assisted Software Development* (2025), version 2025.2, presented by Google Cloud and IT Revolution. 142 pages; no ISBN or DOI. Licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Google LLC). Scope: open-nc.
**Structure:** An unsigned executive summary and a foreword by Gene Kim; signed chapters on software delivery performance and seven team profiles (Nathen Harvey), AI adoption and use (Kevin M. Storer, Derek DeBellis), AI's relationship to key outcomes (DeBellis), the DORA AI Capabilities Model (Storer, DeBellis, Harvey), platform engineering (Eric Maxwell, Benjamin Good), value stream management (Rob Edwards), the AI mirror (Eirini Kalliamvakou), metrics frameworks (Sarah D'Angelo, Ambar Murillo, Sarah Inman, Storer) and final thoughts (Harvey); sidebars by Edward Fraser, Daniella Villalba and Matt Beane; then demographics, methodology (DeBellis, Storer), the research model and its theory (DeBellis), next steps and an appendix of survey items. Evidence: a 4,867-respondent survey (June–July 2025) and 78 interviews (July 2024–July 2025).

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The report's central claim is that AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier: it magnifies the strengths of high-performing organisations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones (p. 3). The greatest returns come from the underlying organisational system (platform quality, clear workflows, aligned teams), without which AI creates local pockets of productivity often lost to downstream chaos (p. 3). Adoption is near-universal (90%), and comparing otherwise similar people, higher AI adoption goes with higher individual effectiveness, organisational, team and product performance, code quality, valuable work and throughput, but also higher instability and no change in burnout or friction (pp. 4, 37–38). DeBellis reads those stubborn results as not entirely a failure of the tool but also of the system to adapt around it: AI's value will be unlocked by reimagining the system of work it inhabits, not by the technology itself (p. 43).

A new DORA AI Capabilities Model names seven capabilities that amplify AI's benefits: a clear and communicated AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control practices, working in small batches, a user-centric focus and quality internal platforms (p. 50). Without a user-centric focus, AI adoption's effect on team performance turns negative (p. 60); platform quality and value stream management each amplify AI's effect on organisational performance (pp. 71, 78). Kalliamvakou frames AI as a mirror and a multiplier of how organisations actually operate, so its adoption should be treated as a transformation (pp. 81, 87). The report offers its findings as hypotheses for readers' own experiments, and its estimates as comparisons rather than effects (pp. 48, 96).

## Executive Summary and Foreword

The summary calls AI adoption a systems problem, not a tools problem, and advises treating it as an organisational transformation that invests in the platform, the data ecosystem and engineering disciplines (p. 5). Developers' trust-but-verify scepticism about AI output is called a sign of mature adoption, and training should teach teams to guide, evaluate and validate AI work rather than simply encourage use (p. 5). Throughput rose with AI this year, a shift from 2024, but instability still rises, which the summary reads as teams adapting for speed while their systems have not yet evolved to manage AI-accelerated development safely (p. 4).

In the foreword, Gene Kim recalls the 2013 State of DevOps research with Nicole Forsgren and Jez Humble, which found that multiple deployments a day were feasible, that reliability seemed to need smaller and more frequent deployments, and that what was needed was good technical practices, architectures allowing independence of action and a learning culture (p. 8). He named the 2024 data's suggestion that more AI meant worse throughput and stability "the DORA 2024 anomaly" (p. 9). With Steve Yegge he defines vibe coding as coding by iterative conversation with an AI, and argues that when AI speeds up development, the people acting as its control system must speed up too, which needs faster feedback loops, architectures with independence of action, and a climate for learning (pp. 9–10). Cases from their book: at Adidas, loosely coupled teams with fast feedback saw 20–30% productivity gains while teams tightly coupled to ERP saw little or no benefit; at Booking.com, training in giving AI explicit instructions and context was the missing ingredient (p. 10). Kim reads both as pointing to the possibility that AI amplifies the strengths and weaknesses of engineering practices (p. 10).

## Software Delivery Performance and Team Profiles

DORA measures throughput (lead time for changes, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, rework rate) for any application or service (p. 13). These are outcomes: they say what is happening, not why, since a low deployment frequency could come from technical debt, bureaucracy or burnout (p. 14). A cluster analysis across eight factors, including well-being measures, yields seven team profiles, whose names the authors call an interpretation of the data (pp. 15–16): Foundational challenges (10%, survival mode), The legacy bottleneck (11%, reacting to unstable systems), Constrained by process (17%, stable systems but a treadmill of inefficient process and burnout), High impact, low cadence (7%, strong product performance with low throughput and high instability), Stable and methodical (15%, steady artisans with lower throughput), Pragmatic performers (20%, fast and stable, average well-being) and Harmonious high-achiever (20%, stable, low-friction and sustainable) (pp. 16–18).

The distribution of the clusters is read as evidence that the speed versus stability trade-off is a myth, with clusters 6 and 7 (nearly 40% of the sample) excelling at both (p. 19). The best comparisons are of the same application over time, and the goal is continuous improvement rather than necessarily top performance (p. 20). In Harvey's hypothetical retrospective, a team notices lead time rising, as likely by simple observation as from a dashboard since precision is not always needed, traces it to slower code reviews, agrees to prioritise reviews and smaller changes, and resolves to look again in a month (p. 22).

## AI Adoption and Use

Ninety percent of respondents use AI at work, up 14.1% on 2024; the median respondent has 16 months of AI experience, and the median AI user spent two hours with AI on their last workday (pp. 24–25). Sixty percent of AI users turn to AI about half the time or more, 65% of AI users rely on it a moderate amount or more, and writing new code is the top use (pp. 26–27). Chatbots and the IDE are the main surfaces, and 61% never use agent mode (p. 29). More than 80% perceive productivity gains and 59% better code quality, while 30% trust AI output little or not at all; the authors conclude absolute trust is not needed for AI output to be useful, and interviewees likened their stance to the healthy scepticism they apply to Stack Overflow solutions, used but not always implicitly trusted (pp. 30–31). A Sabre case note reports 74% adoption, 86% reporting productivity gains, and slow uptake of the newest features such as agent mode (25% of users), answered with training and peer knowledge sharing (p. 26). A UC Berkeley eye-tracking study found student developers used AI for mechanical tasks but largely ignored it, even when accurate, for interpretive tasks; the sidebar concludes AI may add cognitive load there and recommends customising AI tools to the task (p. 28). The authors caution against reading AI's ubiquity as a reason for every organisation to adopt quickly, and urge everyone to think about whether, where and how AI should be applied (p. 32).

## AI and Key Outcomes

Outside surveys show the same rush to adopt and invest, but widespread adoption does not equal widespread value, and adoption can be driven by hype and fear of missing out (pp. 34–35). The 2024 report estimated that each 25% rise in AI adoption cut throughput 1.5% and raised instability 7.2%; a cited METR study of experienced open-source developers using early-2025 AI suggested developers slowed by 19% still believed they were 20% more efficient (pp. 35, 48). AI adoption is measured as one factor of trust, reliance and reflexive use, likely joined by a feedback loop in which trust enables use and use builds trust (p. 36).

The positive associations steady since 2024 (individual effectiveness, code quality, team and organisational performance) are treated as a baseline, not a headline (p. 39). As of now AI tends to turn up at the keyboard, which may explain why code quality and productivity benefit while friction, burnout and instability, properties of the sociotechnical system, do not (p. 39). For the individual, friction moves rather than vanishes, from manual grind to deciding and verifying (p. 40). The findings suggest burnout resists technological fixes and is shaped by work culture; DORA's data tie it to leadership and priority stability, and qualitative signals suggest perceived capacity gains have raised expectations in some organisations (p. 40). Lacking foundational delivery capabilities can neutralise AI's gains; AI is associated with rising instability, DORA found no evidence that AI softens instability's harms, and the authors ask whether the technical capabilities and measures now need to evolve (p. 41). Valuable work, throughput and product performance turned positive since 2024, read as adaptation by people, teams and tools (p. 42). The persistence of the stubborn results is called a failure of the system to adapt around the tool, not of the tool alone (p. 43).

## Developers' Sense of Their Work

Daniella Villalba's sidebar studies six sociocognitive constructs (p. 44). Higher AI adoption goes with greater authentic pride, through more time on valuable work; it shows no effect on meaningful work, need for cognition or existential connection; with 78% certainty it is not associated with a diminished sense of ownership of one's code, AI being wielded as a tool like a compiler, though a 21% probability of decreased ownership remains (pp. 45–46). Higher adopters rate prompt engineering and syntax memorisation as more important, and no other skill, though she is not ready to make conclusions (p. 47). Her takeaway is that AI has not meaningfully changed how developers experience their work, and that developers should see themselves in the driver's seat (p. 47).

## The DORA AI Capabilities Model

From 78 interviews, expert opinion and prior research, 15 candidate capabilities were tested and seven showed substantial evidence of amplifying AI's effects (p. 50). A clear and communicated AI stance amplifies individual effectiveness and organisational performance and turns AI's neutral effect on friction into a decrease; unclear stances are likely to leave some developers too conservative and others too permissive, and the capability measures clarity, not content (pp. 51–53). Healthy data ecosystems amplify organisational performance, and AI-accessible internal data amplifies individual effectiveness and code quality, which may take more than buying licences (pp. 54–55). Frequent commits amplify individual effectiveness and frequent rollback amplifies team performance, version control acting as a psychological safety net; the authors suspect rollback helps by rapidly undoing changes made in larger batches (pp. 56–57). Small batches amplify product performance and reduce friction while slightly reducing AI's boost to individual effectiveness, which the authors argue is a means, not necessarily a goal in itself (p. 58). A user-centric focus amplifies team performance, and without it AI adoption harms team performance (p. 60). Quality internal platforms amplify organisational performance but raise friction, possibly by preventing inappropriate use (p. 62). The chapter's advice runs one item per capability: clarify policy, treat data as an asset, connect AI to internal context, fortify safety nets, shrink work items, centre users, invest in the platform (p. 64).

## Platform Engineering

Platform adoption is 90% and dedicated platform teams 76%; with federated platforms common, the leadership challenge is governing a platform of platforms through loosely coupled teams (pp. 66–67). Users experience the platform as a single entity, so improving one feature in isolation fails; clear feedback on tasks correlates most with a good experience, and user-experience features lag technical ones slightly (pp. 67–69). Three pitfalls are named: build it and they will come, the ticket-ops trap, and the ivory tower platform, each answered by a product approach (p. 68). A quality platform is linked to higher organisational and product performance and productivity, with a small rise in instability read as possibly risk compensation and a manageable trade-off (pp. 66, 70). AI adoption's effect on organisational performance is negligible on low-quality platforms and strong on high-quality ones; the platform scales AI's gains and gives a safe space to experiment, though AI practices should not be over-standardised (pp. 71–72).

## Value Stream Management

Rob Edwards argues that the greatest risk is not falling behind but pouring investment into chaotic activity, and that high performers get better at getting better by understanding their workflow and true constraints (p. 74). VSM is the practice of visualising, analysing and improving the flow of work from idea to customer, through four principles: map the system together, often starting from commit to production after finding the primary constraint; focus on flow, measuring lead time, process time and value-add to wait time, and aim AI at the bottleneck (such as code review) rather than at producing more code; keep an ongoing culture of improvement with clear goals, autonomy, freedom from reprisal and a living record of changes; and build on a platform's paved roads (pp. 74–76). VSM practices go with higher team and product performance and more valuable work, and they dramatically amplify AI's otherwise modest effect on organisational performance (pp. 77–78). The first step is to ask whether the team can draw its value stream on a whiteboard (p. 78).

## The AI Mirror and Skill Development

Eirini Kalliamvakou argues that the environment AI is nested in shapes its impact, and that because the seven capabilities are team- and organisation-level, attention should move from individual use to system design (p. 80). Citing Deming and the Theory of Constraints, she holds that local gains are blocked or absorbed unless the system adapts, as with cloud, Agile and DevOps, so AI adoption needs to be treated as a transformation effort (p. 81). Augmenting existing systems means fixing review, pipeline, data, security and change-management friction, with leaders setting goals and rewarding verification, delegation and orchestration; evolving means AI-native pipelines and collaboration (pp. 82–83). A natural first step is examining how work actually flows, with small cross-functional practitioner groups and executive sponsorship mapping the system, since insight must come from inside the system (pp. 84–85). AI then reflects the organisation: it amplifies flow where systems are aligned and exposes pain points where they are fragmented (p. 87). In his sidebar, Matt Beane reports from more than 31 occupations that default use of intelligent automation lets experts self-serve and leaves novices fewer chances for hands-on work, notes that many organisations focus on measuring AI-related productivity rather than skill development, and urges measuring and optimising both (p. 88).

## Measuring Software Development

The metrics chapter recommends choosing a framework (SPACE, DevEx, HEART, DORA's metrics) by the goals and decisions measurement should serve: developer experience, product excellence or organisational effectiveness (p. 90). Self-reported data capture experience but carry bias; logs-based data scale but need observability, and are not objective (p. 91). For AI, keep existing measures as a baseline and add a few, such as AI suggestion acceptance or trust, rather than overhauling the framework; act on what you measure with leadership sponsorship, through a Plan, Do, Check, Adjust cycle (pp. 92–94). The final chapter calls early standardisation premature, a user-centric focus a prerequisite, and the findings hypotheses to test, warning again against investment in chaotic activity (pp. 95–96).

## Method and Theory

The survey recruited through organic channels and a panel, ran in six languages, and randomly assigned respondents to four topic flows; interviews of about 90 minutes ran continuously and also generated hypotheses (pp. 114–115). The analysis makes causal assumptions explicit in a directed acyclic graph, validates measures by confirmatory factor analysis, checks the whole model by structural equation modelling, and estimates comparisons with Bayesian models under a skeptical prior, reporting 89% credible intervals (pp. 116–127). The research model's pathways hold that service age and criticality shape delivery, well-designed processes reduce coordination overhead and cognitive load, a well-functioning team carries the individual, and environmental demands and resources (including priority stability) shape individual outcomes (pp. 135–136).

## Key Statistics

- 4,867 survey respondents; 78 interviewees (pp. 103, 112).
- 90% use AI at work (+14.1% on 2024); more than 80% perceive productivity gains; 59% perceive better code quality; 30% trust AI output a little or not at all (pp. 24, 30–31).
- 2024 estimate per 25% more AI adoption: throughput −1.5%, instability +7.2% (p. 35).
- Seven capabilities retained from 15 candidates (p. 50).
- 90% have a platform; 76% have a dedicated platform team (p. 67).
- Cluster shares: 10%, 11%, 17%, 7%, 15%, 20%, 20% (pp. 16–18).
- Psychological ownership: 78% certainty not diminished; 21% probability of a decrease (p. 46).
- Never use agent mode: 61% (p. 29).

## Key Connections

- Gene Kim and Steve Yegge, *Vibe Coding*: source of the foreword's definition and the Adidas and Booking.com cases (pp. 9–10).
- Forsgren, Humble and Kim, *Accelerate*, and DORA's own 2024 report, Core Model and guides: cited as continuity (pp. 8–9, 35, 50, 136–137).
- Stack Overflow, Atlassian, LinkedIn, McKinsey, Stanford HAI and METR: cited on adoption, investment and perceived versus measured speed (pp. 34–35).
- A 2019 Microsoft study, Job Demands–Resources theory, a 2017 burnout meta-analysis and the work-intensification literature: cited on friction and burnout (p. 40).
- W. Edwards Deming and the Theory of Constraints: cited for systems thinking (p. 81).
- SPACE, DevEx, HEART and PDCA: measurement frameworks (pp. 90, 94).
- McElreath, *Statistical Rethinking*, and Gelman, Hill and Vehtari, *Regression and Other Stories*: the analysis's methodological base (pp. 48, 115).
- Matt Beane, *The Skill Code*: the skill-development sidebar's author and book (pp. 88, 100, 137).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. The speed versus stability trade-off is a myth (p. 19).
2. Instability is not an acceptable price for AI-enabled throughput; no moderating effect was found (p. 41).
3. AI's ubiquity is not a reason for every organisation to adopt rapidly; the conversation must move from adoption to effective use (pp. 5, 32).
4. Individual effectiveness is a means, not a goal (p. 58).
5. A platform cannot be fixed one feature at a time, and AI practices should not be standardised early (pp. 69, 72, 95).
6. The greatest risk is not falling behind but investment in chaotic activity (pp. 74, 96).
